Psychosis in an Adult: Exclude a Cause, Then Time It Against Mood

How long, which symptoms, only during mood episodes?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

If a mental disorder makes harm to self or others, or unmet basic needs, likely, hospitalize first; involuntarily only if hospital care can help, the patient is unable or unwilling to consent, and it is the least restrictive alternative. Commitment law varies by state. Toxicology, chemistry and TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) help exclude a substance or medical cause. Then time it: brief psychotic disorder is at least 1 of delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech for 1 day to under 1 month, then full return to baseline; schizophreniform disorder is Criterion A for 1 to under 6 months; schizophrenia is Criterion A with functional decline for 6 months or more, 1 month of it active. Delusional disorder is a delusion for at least 1 month, Criterion A never met, and, apart from the delusion’s impact, functioning not markedly impaired and behavior not obviously bizarre; mood episodes, if any, brief relative to it. Each also needs its gate-table exclusions.

Exception: psychosis only during mood episodes is a mood disorder with psychotic features; for schizoaffective disorder, check all three conditions in its gate row.

First tests: what each one rules out
TestOrderResultWhat it rules out

Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
DispositionHospitalize; involuntarily only when the Bottom line conditions and state law allowLikely harm to self or others, or cannot meet basic needs
First lineAntipsychotic at a therapeutic dose; second generation first line in brief psychotic disorderStill ill after an adequate trial (full effect 4 to 6 weeks or more; no minimal gain by 2 weeks predicts little later gain)
Second trialA different antipsychotic; long-acting injectable if nonadherentSymptoms after 2 or more adequate trials, adherence documented

Course and choice by diagnosis
SituationChoice
Brief psychotic disorderContinue the antipsychotic 1 to 3 months after remission (suggested)
Schizophreniform disorderStep down: continue 12 months or longer after symptoms resolve, then taper gradually
Schizophrenia, first episodeContinue at least 1 to 2 years; many years if ill longer
Delusional disorderPsychotherapy that builds trust; a 6-week antipsychotic trial; do not accept the delusion
Follow-up and return precautions Clozapine – ANC before starting, weekly for 6 months, every 2 weeks for the next 6, then monthly, per the prescribing information

Skipped tierClozapine after one failed antipsychotic: resistance needs 2 or more adequate trials with documented adherence.
Complications and long-term sequelae
  • Schizophrenia: lifetime suicide risk 5% to 10%; life expectancy about 15 years shorter.
  • Schizophreniform disorder: may evolve into schizophrenia, bipolar or schizoaffective disorder.
Practice
  1. 52-year-old man brought to the emergency department by police because of odd behavior, after an arrest for disturbing people living nearby; for 6 months he has been pushing flyers hard to promote a New Age healing business he runs from his home, and he claims special abilities that cure every kind of physical and mental illness; he is extremely upset about the arrest and is convinced that the police and the physician are plotting against him and his business; he insists he truly has special powers and could heal everyone in the waiting room; physical examination normal; mental status examination: denies any past psychiatric problems, depression, elevated mood or hearing voices; sleeps 6 to 8 hours a night; laboratory studies within the reference range → Delusional disorder → one delusion for 6 months with no hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms or mood episode
  2. 37-year-old man comes to the physician for strange experiences that began 2 weeks ago, right after his supervisor fired him when he had been expecting a promotion; a security guard watched him clear his desk and walked him out; he then had six drinks at a bar over 4 hours and felt that the other patrons knew about the firing and were watching and discussing him; the feeling was still there when he woke the next day; he drew his curtains and believed people on television were ridiculing him; during the following week he heard a man's voice saying he was a failure who would never amount to anything; he went out only to buy food and wore dark glasses so no one would recognize him; all of it was gone by the end of that week; no serious illness; takes no medications; drinks 2 to 3 beers each night; uses marijuana about once a month; physical examination normal; mental status examination: no hallucinations; thought process logical and goal directed; alert and oriented to person, place and time → Brief psychotic disorder → paranoid delusions and a voice after a stressor, gone within a week and well under 1 month
  3. 24-year-old man brought by his sister because for 3 months he has believed his neighbors implanted a tracking device in his tooth; he hears voices commenting on everything he does and has stopped attending classes; no episodes of depressed or elevated mood; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: flat affect; oriented to person, place and time → Schizophreniform disorder → a delusion plus prominent voices for at least 1 month and under 6 months
  4. 26-year-old man brought by his parents; for 9 months he has heard voices and believed that television hosts send him coded messages; he lost his job, rarely speaks and has stopped bathing; no episodes of depressed or elevated mood; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: flat affect, speech sparse → Schizophrenia → Criterion A symptoms with functional decline for 6 months or more
  5. 46-year-old woman brought by her employer's human resources officer because for 4 months she has written daily letters to a television news anchor she has never met, certain that he is in love with her; she works full time and runs her household without difficulty; no hallucinations; mood normal; sleeps 7 hours a night; vital signs within normal limits; laboratory studies within the reference range → Delusional disorder → an erotomanic delusion for at least 1 month, with functioning intact and no other psychotic or mood symptoms
  6. 34-year-old woman with 1 year of hearing voices that insult her and believing that her coworkers are plotting to poison her; the voices and the belief ran through two episodes during that year, each lasting more than 2 weeks, of depressed mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, excessive guilt and poor concentration nearly every day, which together covered most of the year; the voices and the belief have continued for 4 weeks since her mood returned to normal; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: euthymic mood; full-range affect; hears insulting voices during the interview; alert and oriented to person, place and time → Schizoaffective disorder → Criterion A concurrent with major depressive episodes, 2 weeks or more of delusions and voices without a mood episode, and mood episodes for most of the illness
  7. 29-year-old man brought by his wife after 1 week of sleeping 2 hours a night, talking rapidly and spending their savings; he says God chose him to rule the world; 2 years ago he had a similar week, and his beliefs stopped when his mood settled; he has had no psychotic symptoms between episodes; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: pressured speech; expansive affect; flight of ideas; alert and oriented to person, place and time → Bipolar disorder with psychotic features → the psychosis occurs only during the manic episode
  8. 22-year-old man with 2 days of believing that federal agents are following him; he has smoked methamphetamine every day for the past 3 days and has barely slept; no earlier psychiatric history; HR 96/min; BP 128/80 mm Hg; T 37.0 C; alert and oriented to person, place and time → Substance-induced psychotic disorder → the delusion began during stimulant intoxication; timing ties it to the drug
  9. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of believing that the government has hacked her phone and hearing whispers at night; no past psychiatric history; T 37.0 C; HR 88/min; alert and oriented to person, place and time; neurologic examination normal; serum chemistry panel and TSH normal → Urine toxicology screen → it helps exclude intoxication or withdrawal; imaging needs a neurologic finding or history
  10. 40-year-old man with 10 days of believing his coworkers are poisoning his food; yesterday he bought a knife to confront them; no past psychiatric history; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: oriented to person, place and time → Hospitalization and an antipsychotic → likely harm to others: admit first, whatever the duration; involuntarily if he refuses and no less restrictive option is safe
  11. 27-year-old woman with 2 months of hearing voices and believing that her coworkers read her thoughts; no mood symptoms; not dangerous to herself or others; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative → Antipsychotic and supportive care → psychosis past 1 month is schizophreniform disorder; treatment starts at the first-line rung
  12. 28-year-old woman seen for persecutory delusions and voices that began suddenly after her father's death 7 weeks ago; she was treated with an antipsychotic, and the symptoms are still present; no episodes of depressed or elevated mood; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: guarded; euthymic mood; appears to respond to voices during the interview; alert and oriented to person, place and time → Schizophreniform disorder → the status changed: symptoms past 1 month are no longer brief psychotic disorder
  13. 33-year-old man treated for schizophrenia for 6 years still hears voices daily after adequate trials of risperidone and then olanzapine, with adherence confirmed by pill counts; vital signs within normal limits; mental status examination: flat affect; hears voices during the interview; no suicidal or homicidal ideation; alert and oriented to person, place and time → Clozapine → 2 or more failed adequate trials with documented adherence define treatment resistance
  14. 55-year-old woman treated for 1 month with risperidone and weekly psychotherapy remains certain that her neighbor is poisoning her garden; she works full time and has no hallucinations; vital signs within normal limits → Agreeing that the neighbor is poisoning her garden → accepting the delusion distorts her reality and leads to distrust
  15. 30-year-old man whose voices have persisted for 5 years through adequate, adherent trials of risperidone and olanzapine is about to start clozapine; vital signs within normal limits; complete blood count normal → Neutrophil count weekly for 6 months → then every 2 weeks to month 12, then monthly, per the prescribing information; severe neutropenia risk is highest early
  16. 32-year-old woman admitted 3 weeks ago with 10 days of persecutory delusions and voices after her house burned down was started on risperidone; every symptom resolved 1 week ago; vital signs within normal limits; urine toxicology negative → Continue it 1 to 3 months, then reassess → remission within 1 month: continuing 1 to 3 months after remission is suggested
How NBME framed it: question 1 The stem pairs a 6-month healing business with a belief that the police and the physician are conspiring against him, then clears every other symptom: no voices, no depressed or elevated mood, normal sleep and normal labs. NBME’s explanation says delusional disorder has no other psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations; current criteria allow hallucinations that are not prominent and are tied to the delusional theme, which this stem does not test.
Distractors: NBME question 1
Unchecked attributeSchizophrenia: his 6 months fit, but Criterion A needs a second symptom beside the delusion; he has an isolated delusion, no disorganization, hallucinations or negative symptoms.
True-fact-wrong-slotBipolar disorder: mood episodes can carry delusions, but he reports no depressed or euphoric mood and sleeps 6 to 8 hours.
Unchecked attributeBrief psychotic disorder: an acute psychosis, but it lasts under 1 month; his delusion has lasted 6 months.
Salient decoySchizoaffective disorder: his distress and aggressive leafleting hint at mood, but he has no mood episode and no second Criterion A symptom.
How NBME framed it: question 2 The stem wraps a week of paranoid delusions and one voice in a firing, a night of drinking and monthly cannabis, so a stressor disorder (adjustment disorder, PTSD) and a substance cause sit beside the psychotic disorders. The explanation removes each by its own feature: psychosis is atypical in adjustment disorder, there was no life-threatening event, alcohol rarely causes psychosis, and 1 week is too short for delusional or schizophreniform disorder.
Distractors: NBME question 2
Unchecked attributeDelusional disorder: paranoid delusions fit, but it needs at least 1 month; his symptoms lasted 1 week.
Unchecked attributeSchizophreniform disorder: two psychotic symptoms fit, but it needs at least 1 month and under 6 months.
Salient decoySubstance-induced psychotic disorder: he drank that night, but alcohol rarely causes psychosis directly and his cannabis use is intermittent.
True-fact-wrong-slotAdjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct: a stressor within 3 months fits, but psychotic symptoms would be atypical.
Salient decoyPTSD: losing a job is not a life-threatening event, and he had no intrusive memories, no avoidance of reminders and no change in mood.
Pairs with Mania with psychotic features: does the psychosis occur only during a manic episode? Delirium: does it occur only during a delirium?
Transferable rules

In a new psychosis, settle the level of care, exclude a substance or medical cause, then ask how long the psychotic symptoms have lasted and whether they occur only during mood episodes.

A delusion for at least 1 month, with schizophrenia’s Criterion A never met, functioning not markedly impaired apart from the delusion, behavior not obviously bizarre, any mood episodes brief relative to it, and no substance, medical or other mental disorder to explain it, is delusional disorder.

Elevated or Irritable Mood: Mania, Hypomania, and What to Start or Stop

Psychiatry · DIGFAST · how long, how impaired, and is anything else causing it?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

Elevated or irritable mood with more energy and at least 3 DIGFAST symptoms (4 if only irritable), for 1 week or more or any length if hospitalized, is a manic episode; one makes bipolar I disorder. Mania needs psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization; hypomania (4 days or more) has none of the three. A urine drug screen and TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) help exclude a stimulant or thyroid cause. Hospitalize when needed to prevent harm, stop any antidepressant, and start lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic.

Exception: grandiose delusions do not make it schizophrenia when they occur only during the manic episode.

Illness script
Bipolar I disorder
What it isAt least 1 manic episode; depression is not required but occurs in most
TriggersFamily history: heritability 70 to 90% (strongest, non-modifiable); childhood maltreatment; childbirth, divorce; an antidepressant can switch to mania
WhoOnset usually in the teens to 30s, peaks at 15 to 24 and 45 to 54; men and women equally
LooksDIGFAST symptoms; grandiose delusions in some
CourseRecurrent; maintenance for many years, possibly lifelong
How it hides in a stem
Question 1 stem (the car rental office): what each clue points to

Normal vital signsNot alcohol withdrawal (autonomic instability)
Normal laboratory studiesNo medical cause found ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Diagnosis
Manic episode criteria, as PsychDB lists them Mood: abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable, and increased activity or energy · Duration: at least 1 week, most of the day, nearly every day, or any duration if hospitalization is necessary · Symptoms: at least 3 DIGFAST symptoms, 4 if the mood is only irritable · Severity: marked impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm to self or others, or psychotic features · Cause: not a substance or medical condition; a full episode that outlasts an antidepressant’s effect still counts · Bipolar I: at least 1 manic episode; a depressive episode is not required
DIGFAST
  • Distractibility – attention too easily drawn to irrelevant stimuli
  • Indiscretion – painful consequences: buying sprees, sexual behaviours, foolish business investments
  • Grandiosity – inflated self-esteem
  • Flight of ideas – thoughts are racing
  • Activity increased – goal-directed, or psychomotor agitation
  • Sleep decreased – feels rested after only 3 hours
  • Talkativeness – pressure to keep talking
Timeline gates: which episode, which disorder
Episode or disorderRequired symptomsDurationSeverityDeciding feature
Manic episode3 or more DIGFAST (4 if only irritable)1 week or more; any if hospitalizedImpairment, hospitalization or psychosisOne makes bipolar I
Hypomanic episodeSame count; others notice the change4 consecutive days or moreNone of the threePsychosis makes it manic
Bipolar II disorderAt least 1 hypomanic and 1 major depressive episodeAs for each episodeNever a manic episodeAny mania makes it bipolar I
Cyclothymic disorderUp and down periods below full criteriaMore than 2 yearsNo full episode of any kindSwings never reach an episode
With mixed featuresFull mania or hypomania plus at least 3 depressive symptomsThat of the episodeThat of the episodeGuilt, sadness, thoughts of death in mania
First tests: what each one rules out
TestOrderResultWhat it rules out
Urine drug screenFirstNegativeHelps exclude a stimulant cause
Positive for amphetamine or cocaineStimulant cause: review the timing of use
TSH and free thyroxineFirstNormalHyperthyroidism
CBC (complete blood count), basic metabolic panelFirstNormalOther medical conditions
Pregnancy test, woman of childbearing ageBy branchPositive or negativePregnancy, before choosing a mood stabilizer
Other causes of grandiosity and agitation
DiagnosisThe stem showsDecides itRules out
SchizophreniaGrandiose delusions, odd behaviorPsychosis outside mood episodesPsychosis only during mania
Histrionic personality disorderSeductive, theatrical, attention seekingChronic, pervasive patternSeductive only during an episode
Delusional disorderA fixed grandiose beliefDelusion without maniaDIGFAST symptoms beside the delusion
Brief psychotic disorderSudden psychosisPsychosis lasting under 1 monthPsychosis secondary to mania
ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder)Hyperactive, impulsiveChronic, in more than one settingAcute onset with manic symptoms
Alcohol withdrawal deliriumFound wandering, hallucinatingAutonomic instability, tremor, confusionNormal vital signs; fully oriented
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute manic episode
TierInterventionEscalate when
DispositionPsychiatric hospitalization, often needed: mania is an emergencyNeeded to prevent harm to self or others
Every patientAssess violence and self-harm risk; stop antidepressants, stimulants, alcoholNot gated: with first line
First lineLithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic (quetiapine, aripiprazole, risperidone), alone or combinedNo improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses: check adherence and substance use
Add on or switchAdd or switch to another first-line agentNo improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses
Severe or resistantElectroconvulsive therapy may be consideredTop rung

Step down: after remission, maintenance for all patients with bipolar I disorder, continuous rather than intermittent, for many years, possibly lifelong.

Choice by situation
SituationChoice
Severe agitation or manic psychosisSedating second-generation antipsychotic, sometimes lorazepam at first
Woman of childbearing potentialNo valproate: teratogenic
Maintenance, first lineLithium (lowers suicide risk), quetiapine, divalproex, lamotrigine (weak against mania), aripiprazole
Bipolar I depressionQuetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone; no antidepressant monotherapy
Follow-up and return precautions Maintenance – continuous, not intermittent · Depressive episode – assess suicide risk first; most suicide deaths in bipolar disorder occur then
Distractors
True-fact-wrong-slotContinue the antidepressant, add a mood stabilizer: antidepressants are stopped in mania.
Class-vs-memberValproate in a woman of childbearing potential: right class, disqualified member.
Sequencing trapLithium alone for severe agitation: it takes 4 to 10 days to work.
Calendar trapSwitching after 4 days: judge response at 2 weeks of therapeutic doses.
True-fact-wrong-slotSSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) monotherapy for bipolar depression: risks a switch to mania.
Complications and long-term sequelae
  • During the episode: mania disrupts function and endangers safety.
  • Over the lifetime: suicide rate about 20 to 30 times the general population’s; about 13 years of life lost.
Practice
  1. 24-year-old woman brought to the emergency department by police after she swore loudly at a clerk at a car rental counter; the clerk phoned police for help when she became “out of control” on hearing that no luxury sports cars were available to rent; she works as a receptionist at a local accounting office; physical examination normal; during the examination she requests the physician’s phone number, winks and tells the physician, “I could really show you a good time,” then tries to kiss the physician; mental status examination: agitated; she says she feels “absolutely fantastic!”; speech loud and rapid; asked about the rental counter, she says anyone can see she is fabulously wealthy and the rental staff will regret it if they make her late for her upcoming television interview; urine toxicology screening negative → Bipolar disorder → euphoric, irritable mood with rapid speech, sexual indiscretion, overspending and grandiose delusions: acute mania
  2. 43-year-old man admitted for treatment of superficial frostbite of the toes; police found him 5 hours earlier walking barefoot through a snowstorm; he says he is a god who can melt the snow and purify the heart; he gives the date and his location correctly; asked to recall three words (red, penny, train), he laughs, then playfully answers, “color, coin, conveyance”; speech rapid and incessant; he paces the examination room, arms raised overhead, pointing both index fingers upward; vital signs and laboratory studies within normal limits → Bipolar disorder, manic → grandiose delusion, rapid incessant speech and more activity with normal vital signs and full orientation; the psychosis is secondary to mania
  3. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of sleeping 4 hours a night without feeling tired, talking faster than usual and starting three new projects at work; coworkers have noticed the change; she is still working and meeting deadlines; 2 years ago she was treated for a major depressive episode; T 36.8 C, HR 78/min; urine toxicology negative; TSH normal; mental status examination: mildly elevated mood, rapid but interruptible speech, no delusions or hallucinations → Bipolar II disorder → 4 or more days of symptoms others notice, without marked impairment or psychosis, plus a past major depressive episode
  4. 27-year-old man brought to the emergency department after walking into highway traffic, laughing; for 3 days he has not slept, has spent his savings on a sailboat and talks without pause; he is admitted to the psychiatric unit because of the danger to himself; no delusions or hallucinations; no previous mood episodes; HR 96/min, BP 132/80 mm Hg; urine toxicology negative; TSH normal; mental status examination: expansive mood, pressured speech, flight of ideas, oriented to person, place and time → Bipolar I disorder → hospitalization satisfies both the duration and the severity criteria, so 3 days is enough
  5. 29-year-old man with 9 days of sleeping 3 hours a night, rapid speech and new business plans; he believes God has chosen him as a prophet to lead the nation; he still goes to work each day; 1 year ago he had a major depressive episode; HR 84/min, BP 126/80 mm Hg; urine toxicology negative; TSH normal; mental status examination: expansive mood, pressured speech, grandiose delusion, no hallucinations → Bipolar I disorder → psychotic features make the episode manic by definition, even while he keeps working
  6. 38-year-old woman brought by her husband after 10 days of sleeping 2 to 3 hours a night, racing thoughts, nonstop talking, irritability and $9,000 of online purchases; she has stopped going to work; throughout this time she has cried daily, calls herself a terrible mother and has recurrent thoughts of death without a plan; 5 years ago she was hospitalized for a similar week of elevated mood; HR 88/min, BP 124/78 mm Hg; urine toxicology negative; mental status examination: irritable mood, pressured speech, tearful labile affect, flight of ideas, oriented to person, place and time → Bipolar I disorder, manic episode with mixed features → full manic criteria plus at least 3 depressive symptoms (depressed mood, guilt, thoughts of death)
  7. 26-year-old woman started sertraline 4 weeks ago for a first major depressive episode; for 8 days she has slept 3 hours a night, talks rapidly, has quit her job to launch three businesses and says she is destined to be famous; HR 92/min, BP 118/74 mm Hg; urine toxicology negative; TSH normal; urine pregnancy test negative; mental status examination: euphoric mood, pressured speech, grandiose delusion, no suicidal thoughts → Stop sertraline and start quetiapine → a full manic episode on an antidepressant: stop the antidepressant and start a first-line agent

Psychiatry · safety, stressor, family, adherence, engagement, work · what is driving this relapse or limiting recovery, and which added treatment answers it?

Bottom line

Every patient with schizophrenia stays on an antipsychotic, with psychosocial treatment added to it. When a patient who is receiving his doses gets worse, find what changed in his life before changing the drug. A family conflict just before the worsening calls for family therapy first; a higher dose or dosing frequency is considered after that.

Exception: danger to himself or others can require hospitalization, involuntary if necessary.

Why a family conflict worsens psychosis: stress increases the negative meaning a patient gives his hallucinations and lowers the emotional reserve he has for coping with them, and his daily functioning suffers.

  • Other triggers to ask about: substance use, especially cannabis; becoming unemployed or impoverished; leaving home for college; the end of a romantic relationship.

Delirium: Tell It From Dementia and Psychosis, Then Find the Cause

Psychiatry · onset, attention, fluctuation, orientation · did attention fail over hours to days, and which drug or illness caused it?

Red flagsScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPreventionComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

A disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to a few days and fluctuates through the day is delirium; delusions and hallucinations can be part of it. Dementia begins slowly with attention spared until it is severe, and a new psychosis in an older adult usually indicates delirium or dementia. Review every drug first: anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines are common causes, and meperidine is among the most deliriogenic opioids. Stop the offending drug, treat the medical cause, reorient the patient and protect sleep. An antipsychotic is only for severe agitation that threatens safety.

Exception: delirium from alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal is treated with an IV benzodiazepine; in every other delirium, benzodiazepines are avoided.

Panic Disorder and Its Mimics: Which Anxiety, and How to Treat

Psychiatry · panic disorder criteria · are the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?

Bottom line

Recurrent unexpected panic attacks, with at least 1 month of worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behavior, are panic disorder once a substance and a medical cause are excluded. Order a TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), glucose and urine toxicology, and consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) for palpitations or chest pain; no test makes the diagnosis. Treat with CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both; start the drug low and titrate slowly. A benzodiazepine is short term only.

Exception: attacks that come only in feared social situations or with one feared object or situation are social anxiety disorder or specific phobia.

SSRI (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor) Adverse Effects: Name the Effect, Then Take the Next Step

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPreventionPractice
Bottom line

Sexual dysfunction affects more than half of patients on an SSRI and can reach desire, arousal or orgasm. When low desire is persistent and distressing and the depression is in sustained remission, first lower the dose. If that fails, a patient with one episode may taper off; one who wants to stay on an antidepressant adds bupropion or switches to bupropion or mirtazapine. Another SSRI carries a similar risk, and sildenafil can help arousal problems and anorgasmia, yet no effect on desire has been shown.

Exception: flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances or hyperarousal within 3 days of stopping or starting a taper are discontinuation syndrome, not relapse: reassure, and if they began during a taper, consider restarting the original dose and tapering more slowly.

The Patient on Lithium: Which Complication, and What to Do

Psychiatry · sodium with urine osmolality, lithium level, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) · is this toxicity, diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism or an expected effect?

Red flagsScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementMonitoringPractice
Bottom line

On lithium with new symptoms, read three pairs together: serum sodium with urine osmolality, lithium level with the neurologic examination, TSH with free thyroxine. A high sodium with dilute urine after years of lithium is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: replete volume, and stop lithium if possible. Coarse tremor, slurred speech, ataxia or confusion with a raised level is toxicity (commonly above 1.5 mmol/L; lower in chronic toxicity): stop lithium, give IV isotonic fluids, and dialyze for decreased consciousness, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia. A high TSH with a low free thyroxine is hypothyroidism: add levothyroxine and continue lithium. A mildly high TSH with a normal free thyroxine and no symptoms is the routine thyroid change.

Suspect IPV (intimate partner violence) when frequent injuries come with explanations that do not fit, and/or when bruises sit in a suspicious distribution: lower abdomen, back or forearms.   9. 30-year-old woman in the emergency department with swollen, tender forearms and bruises along both forearms 1 day after what she calls a trip over a rug; third injury visit this year; HR 92/min, BP 124/80 mm Hg; alert and oriented to person, place and time; anxious affect → Raising the arms to shield the face and torso → defensive movements during an attack bruise the forearms
  10. 35-year-old woman who told the physician 1 month ago that her husband hits her, and who made a safety plan then, returns alone for a blood pressure check; BP 128/82 mm Hg, HR 76/min; no new injuries; alert and oriented to person, place and time; euthymic mood → Ask again, privately, about her current safety → assess the risk of immediate harm at every visit
  11. 31-year-old woman in the emergency department 2 hours after her husband slapped her and shoved her against a wall; she wants to go home tonight; no history of psychiatric illness; T 37.0 C, HR 96/min, BP 124/78 mm Hg; bruises on her upper arms and back; slightly disheveled; tearful, anxious mood; denies suicidal or homicidal ideation; alert and oriented to person, place and time; insight and judgment intact → Develop an emergency safety plan with her → the danger is her home, not a psychiatric condition: judgment intact and no suicidal ideation; a competent adult decides when to leave
  12. 81-year-old woman with dementia brought to the clinic by her husband, who is her caregiver; bruises on both upper arms; he says she falls, but her gait is steady on examination; HR 78/min, BP 132/80 mm Hg; oriented to person only; cannot name the year; poor insight and judgment → Report the abuse to Adult Protective Services → she cannot decide for herself, so seeing her alone cannot yield a plan she can carry out; most states require reporting the abuse of older adults, and waiting for a follow-up visit leaves her with the suspected abuser
Distractors: the NBME question
True-fact-wrong-slotAdmission to an inpatient psychiatric facility: she is in danger, but from her home situation, not a psychiatric condition; admission removes her only for a while.
Sequencing trapContacting the police: some states may require it, but it is not the first step; before she can leave safely it may escalate the violence.
Uniform-answer doubtAn emergency safety plan (the key): it looks too modest for a third fracture, but all patients get help with one, whether or not they disclose abuse.
True-fact-wrong-slotAnger management therapy for the husband: he is the source, but therapy has not conclusively been shown to lower the risk of violence.
Sequencing trapAn order of protection against the husband: filed before she is willing and able to leave safely, it may increase the risk of harm.
How NBME framed it The stem never says abuse: it shows repeated injuries, an apologetic story that does not match the bruises, and a patient who often looks at her husband before she answers. The lead-in asks for the first course of action, and four options act through the police, the courts, a psychiatric unit or the husband, so only the safety plan acts with her.
Pairs with Part I Elder Abuse & Mandated Reporting covers the older adult who cannot protect herself, where suspicion alone leads to a report. Ask: can the injured adult decide for herself? Part II Suspected Child Abuse: Fractures and the Next Step covers the injured child. Ask: is the person being harmed a child?
Transferable rule

When a competent adult is being hurt at home, the first action is one she can use today: ask her alone, then build a safety plan with her, whatever she discloses. Reporting follows who is at risk and state law, and it is not the first step for her own abuse.

Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder (Vaginismus): Exclude a Body Cause, Then Treat

Female sexual dysfunction · criteria held for about 6 months · is it pelvic floor tightening with fear of pain, or a cause the examination finds?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Persistent difficulty with vaginal penetration, from pain, fear of pain or pelvic floor muscles that tighten on the attempt, lasting about 6 months with distress, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (GPPPD), the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition) diagnosis that took in vaginismus. Examine before labeling it: inspect the vulva, map any pain with a cotton swab, and palpate the pelvic floor with one finger. Test a discharge if there is one.

Treatment is multimodal: pelvic floor physical therapy, psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and psychoeducation.

Exception: pain deep in the pelvis with painful periods is not an entry problem; it points to endometriosis.

Illness script
Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder
What it isPersistent difficulty with attempted or completed vaginal penetration
DriverInvoluntary contraction of the pelvic floor muscles on attempted penetration
TriggersA history of abuse, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; not every patient has one
Secondary toA vulvar infection such as candidiasis, endometriosis or pregnancy
LooksCannot have intercourse or insert a tampon or speculum; anxious before sex
ExaminationNormal apart from pelvic floor tightness
How it hides in a stem
History: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
A woman of 23Premenopausal: atrophy is unlikely ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Came for a contraceptive refillRaised at a routine visit, not repeated care-seeking ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Sexually active with two partnersInterest in sex is intact ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Cannot have intercourse because of painCriterion A: penetration difficulty and pain
Anxious before sexual activityCriterion A: fear of pain; tied to sex, not general worry
Pelvic floor contracts and blocks penetrationCriterion A: pelvic floor tightening
Cannot use tamponsAny penetration fails, not only intercourse ⚠︎ (role inferred)
No sexual traumaA risk factor absent; the diagnosis does not need one ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Examination
ClueWhat it points to
Vital signs normalNo systemic illness ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Speculum hard to advancePelvic floor tightness, the one abnormal finding expected
Diagnosis
DSM-5 criteria A: persistent or recurrent difficulty with one or more of: vaginal penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during intercourse or penetration attempts; marked fear or anxiety about that pain before, during or as a result of penetration; marked tensing or tightening of the pelvic floor muscles on attempted penetration · B: about 6 months or longer · C: clinically significant distress · D: not better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or other significant stressors, and not due to a substance, a medication or another medical condition

Criteria as listed by the University of British Columbia Sexual Health Research group; Merck Manual Professional gives the DSM-5-TR (text revision) version as at least 6 months with significant distress.

First tests: examine before labeling
TestOrderResultRules in or out
Vulvar inspectionFirstAtrophy, redness, lesions, discolorationA body cause: criterion D
Normal vulvaFits GPPPD
Cotton swab mapping, hymen includedFirstPain at the vestibuleProvoked vestibulodynia
Single-digit vaginal examinationFirstPelvic floor contracts or is tenderPelvic floor dysfunction, as in GPPPD
Discharge testing, if discharge, burning or odorBy branchOrganisms on microscopyVaginitis such as candidiasis
Rectovaginal examination, if pain is deepBy branchCul-de-sac nodularityEndometriosis
Transvaginal ultrasonography, if a mass is feltBy branchA myoma or other massA structural cause of deep pain
Other causes of painful or blocked penetration
DiagnosisThe stem showsDeciding featureSettled by
VulvodyniaVulvar pain for 3 months or moreNo identifiable cause; swab maps the painCotton swab test after excluding other causes
Vaginal candidiasisRecent antibiotics, diabetes, immunosuppressionRed, swollen vulva; thick white dischargeMicroscopy of the discharge
Genitourinary syndrome of menopausePostmenopausal burning and drynessPale, dry tissueInspection
Lichen sclerosusBurning, dryness, itchingVisible skin changesInspection; biopsy if needed
EndometriosisDeep pain; painful periods commonCul-de-sac nodularityRectovaginal examination
Female sexual interest/arousal disorderLittle interest or arousalAt least 3 of 6 symptomsCriteria: 6 months, distress
Major depressive disorderLow mood, lost interestLow mood or anhedonia beyond sexFive symptoms in the same 2 weeks
Generalized anxiety disorderWorry about many topicsAnxiety not limited to penetration6 months or more of worry plus 3 symptoms
Somatic symptom disorderPreoccupied with symptoms; repeated visitsExcessive time and energy on symptomsHistory of health-seeking
Management and treatment
Multimodal treatment: the parts are combined, not stepped
PartAims atWhat the source says
Pelvic floor physical therapyPelvic muscle relaxationPrimary; considered an effective intervention
Psychotherapy such as CBT; sex therapyFear and anxiety about painPrimary; CBT is strongly recommended
PsychoeducationUnderstanding the disorderPrimary part of treatment
Sequential vaginal dilatorsTight pelvic musclesPart of multidisciplinary care
Topical lidocaine before sexPainFor a short time only

The sources give no fixed order or failure interval between these parts, so there is no escalation ladder here.

When the examination finds a body cause
FindingTreatment
Postmenopausal, pale, dry tissueVaginal estrogen, the most effective therapy when symptomatic; lubricants may give temporary relief
Lichen sclerosusUsually topical steroids
VulvodyniaGentle vulvar care, physical therapy; vestibulectomy may help only after nonsurgical options fail, with pain localized to the vestibule
EndometriosisNonopioid analgesics, combined oral contraceptives or progestogens; laparoscopic excision
Distractors
Unchecked attributeVulvodynia: both hurt at the entrance; vulvodynia is vulvar pain the swab maps, and it does not explain muscles that clamp shut.
True-fact-wrong-slotVaginal candidiasis: it is associated with vaginismus; without redness, swelling or thick white discharge it is not the cause.
Salient decoyGeneralized anxiety disorder: the patient is anxious; her anxiety is about penetration, not many topics.
Salient decoySomatic symptom disorder: the complaint is pain; she is not preoccupied with it or seeking care again and again.
True-fact-wrong-slotVaginal estrogen in a young woman: it treats pale, dry postmenopausal tissue, not a tight pelvic floor.
Sequencing trapVestibulectomy: it belongs to vulvodynia localized to the vestibule, and only after nonsurgical treatment has failed.
Practice
  1. 23-year-old woman at a follow-up clinic visit asking for a refill of her oral contraceptive pills; she has sex with two male partners, yet pain has kept her from having vaginal intercourse; she feels anxious ahead of any sexual activity and senses her pelvic floor muscles tighten and block penetration; she has also been unable to insert tampons; no history of sexual trauma; vital signs within normal limits; on pelvic examination the speculum is hard to advance into the vagina → Vaginismus → pain, fear before sex and a pelvic floor that tightens to block penetration; DSM-5 now calls it genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder
  2. 38-year-old woman with 5 months of burning pain of the vulva most of the day, whether or not she is sexually active; she can have intercourse and insert tampons, though the burning persists; regular menses; T 36.8 C, HR 74/min, BP 118/72 mm Hg; the vulva looks normal, with no discharge, redness or skin change; touching the vulva with a cotton swab reproduces burning in several areas; single-digit examination finds a relaxed, nontender pelvic floor; microscopy of vaginal fluid shows no yeast; euthymic mood → Vulvodynia → vulvar pain for at least 3 months with no identifiable cause; the pelvic floor is relaxed and penetration is possible
  3. 24-year-old woman with 4 days of vulvar itching and burning pain during intercourse; she had no pain with intercourse before this week; she finished a course of amoxicillin for sinusitis 1 week ago; T 37.0 C, HR 80/min, BP 116/74 mm Hg; the vulva and vagina are red and swollen, with a thick white discharge; calm, euthymic mood → Vaginal candidiasis → redness, swelling and thick white discharge after antibiotics; microscopy of the discharge confirms, and 4 days is far short of the 6 months GPPPD needs
  4. 35-year-old woman with 8 months of no interest in sex; she has stopped having sexual thoughts, no longer initiates and is usually unreceptive when her husband does; during sex she feels little excitement or pleasure; no pain with penetration and no fear of it; she is distressed by the change; she sleeps well and still enjoys her work and hobbies; T 36.8 C, HR 70/min, BP 114/72 mm Hg; pelvic examination normal, with a relaxed pelvic floor; euthymic mood, full affect, no suicidal ideation → Female sexual interest/arousal disorder → at least 3 of the 6 interest and arousal symptoms for 6 months with distress; no pain, and no low mood or anhedonia beyond sex
  5. 27-year-old woman with 7 months of being unable to have intercourse with her partner; it began after a yeast infection that was treated 8 months ago; she now dreads any attempt, and her pelvic floor clamps down as soon as penetration is tried; she is distressed and wants to resume intercourse; T 36.9 C, HR 82/min, BP 110/70 mm Hg; the vulva looks normal, with no discharge; microscopy shows no yeast; single-digit examination sets off involuntary pelvic floor contraction; anxious affect when discussing sex → Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder → fear and pelvic floor tightening for about 6 months with distress; it can follow a vulvar infection, and a clear microscopy excludes active infection
  6. 26-year-old woman with 8 months of pain at the vaginal opening during every attempt at intercourse, and fear before each attempt; she is distressed; she has never had a pelvic examination; T 36.8 C, HR 78/min, BP 116/74 mm Hg; she is anxious and asks to go slowly → Vulvar inspection, cotton swab testing and a single-digit examination → entry pain is examined first: inspection finds a body cause, the swab maps vestibular pain and one finger finds a tight pelvic floor
  7. 22-year-old woman with 1 year of being unable to have intercourse or insert a tampon; she fears the pain and feels her muscles clamp down whenever penetration is tried; she is distressed and wants intercourse with her partner; T 36.9 C, HR 76/min, BP 112/70 mm Hg; the vulva looks normal; cotton swab testing is not painful; microscopy of vaginal fluid is normal; single-digit examination sets off involuntary pelvic floor contraction; anxious affect → Pelvic floor physical therapy with cognitive behavioral therapy → genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder: treatment is multimodal, aimed at the pelvic floor and the fear
  8. 58-year-old woman whose last menstrual period was 7 years ago has 1 year of vaginal dryness and burning with intercourse; lubricants help only briefly; she wants to stay sexually active; T 36.7 C, BP 128/80 mm Hg; the vaginal tissue is pale and dry; no discharge; the pelvic floor is relaxed and nontender; euthymic mood → Low-dose vaginal estrogen → pale, dry postmenopausal tissue: vaginal estrogen is the most effective therapy for symptomatic women
  9. 25-year-old woman with 9 months of being unable to tolerate intercourse or a speculum examination; she tenses and pulls away as the speculum nears the vagina; T 37.0 C, BP 114/72 mm Hg; the vulva and vestibule look normal; cotton swab testing is not painful; microscopy of vaginal fluid is normal; anxious affect → Involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor muscles → the levator ani contracts on attempted penetration; the tissue itself is normal
Distractors: the NBME question
Salient decoyGeneralized anxiety disorder: she is anxious, but that needs 6 months or more of excessive worry about many topics with 3 more symptoms; hers is limited to vaginal penetration.
Salient decoySomatic symptom disorder: the complaint is pain, but there is no excessive preoccupation or repeated health-seeking outside attempted penetration.
True-fact-wrong-slotVaginal candidiasis: associated with vaginismus, but it shows vulvar and vaginal redness, swelling and thick white discharge, and the stem gives no antibiotic use, diabetes or immunosuppression.
Unchecked attributeVulvodynia: vulvar pain without an identifiable cause; the swab maps it, and it does not explain a pelvic floor that contracts to prevent penetration.
Uniform-answer doubtVaginismus (the key): it looks like a symptom rather than a diagnosis, but pain, fear and pelvic floor tightening on penetration are its defining features.
How NBME framed it The stem hides the complaint in a contraceptive refill visit and lists the criteria as her experience: pain, anxiety before sex and muscles that block penetration, with a speculum that will not pass; it gives no duration and uses the older term vaginismus. NBME's explanation says vulvodynia is vulvar rather than vaginal pain and is not typically provoked by penetration; the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) classes some vulvodynia as provoked by insertion, so the page separates the two by where the problem is (vulvar skin mapped by the swab versus a contracting pelvic floor).
Transferable rule

When penetration hurts or fails, examine first: a finding on inspection, swab or microscopy names a body cause. A normal examination with fear of pain and a pelvic floor that contracts is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, treated with pelvic floor therapy and psychotherapy together.
